# Search a table with full-text search
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/full-text-search

Use pg_pinecone to keep a Pinecone index for full-text search in sync with a Postgres table, then run BM25, filtered, and hybrid searches in SQL.

pg\_pinecone can keep a Pinecone index for [full-text search](/guides/search/full-text-search) in sync with a Postgres table's text columns. You declare the searchable columns once and search them with SQL, and Postgres stays the system of record.

## Before you begin

* pg\_pinecone installed, as the [quickstart](/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart) shows.
* A Pinecone API key stored in the database. Store it with `SELECT pinecone.set_api_key('YOUR_API_KEY');`.
* `pg_pinecone` in `shared_preload_libraries`, followed by a Postgres restart. See [Preload the extension](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote#preload-the-extension).
* A table with a single-column primary key, which becomes each document's ID. You must own the table.

## Search a table

### 1. Create a sample table

This guide uses a table of help-center articles. The embeddings are only needed to [combine text and vector search](#combine-text-and-vector-search):

```sql SQL theme={null}
CREATE TABLE articles (
    id        bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text,
    body      text,
    category  text,
    embedding vector(1024)
);

WITH input(id, title, body, category) AS (
    VALUES
        (1, 'Reset your password', 'Open Settings, choose Security, and select Reset password. A reset link arrives by email within a few minutes.', 'account'),
        (2, 'Enable two-factor authentication', 'Two-factor authentication adds a one-time code from an authenticator app to every sign-in.', 'account'),
        (3, 'Export your data', 'Go to Settings and choose Export to download every project as a CSV file.', 'data'),
        (4, 'Fix error E-1042 during import', 'Error E-1042 means the CSV file has a header row that does not match the table columns.', 'data'),
        (5, 'Change your billing plan', 'Upgrade or downgrade your plan from the Billing page. Changes take effect at the next invoice.', 'billing'),
        (6, 'Download past invoices', 'Every invoice is available as a PDF on the Billing page under Invoice history.', 'billing')
)
INSERT INTO articles (id, title, body, category, embedding)
SELECT i.id, i.title, i.body, i.category, e.embedding::vector
FROM input i
JOIN pinecone.embed_batch((SELECT array_agg(title || '. ' || body ORDER BY id) FROM input)) e
  ON e.ordinal = i.id;
```

### 2. Declare the searchable columns

Call `pinecone.track_docs()` with the text columns to index. `metadata_columns` lists columns you want to filter on, and `vector_column` is optional. `text_columns` takes a JSON list, and `metadata_columns` takes a Postgres array:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.track_docs(
    'articles',
    text_columns     => '["title", "body"]',
    metadata_columns => ARRAY['category'],
    vector_column    => 'embedding'
);
```

This creates a Pinecone index and queues the table's existing rows to be copied to it. Only the declared columns leave Postgres. From then on, pg\_pinecone copies every committed insert, update, and delete in the background.

A list of column names uses English text analysis with stemming and stop words. To set options per column, pass an object instead. For example, on a table with a `sku` column, turn off stemming and stop words so identifiers match exactly:

```sql SQL theme={null}
text_columns => '{"title": {"language": "en"}, "sku": {"stemming": false, "stop_words": false}}'
```

### 3. Wait for the initial copy

Check progress with `pinecone.status()`:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT table_name, docs_backfill_done, docs_backfill_total, docs_queue_state
FROM pinecone.status();
```

The copy is finished when `docs_backfill_done` equals `docs_backfill_total`. `pinecone.flush_docs('articles')` waits until everything committed so far has been delivered, then returns `true`. It returns `false` if delivery doesn't finish within 30 seconds. Pinecone then takes up to about a minute to index delivered documents and make them searchable.

### 4. Search the table

`pinecone.search_docs()` returns each match's ID, score, and rank. Join back to the table for the rest of the row:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT a.id, a.title, s.score
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'download invoice pdf', k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

```text Output theme={null}
 id |          title           |   score
----+--------------------------+-----------
  6 | Download past invoices   |  6.580365
  3 | Export your data         | 1.6908139
  5 | Change your billing plan | 1.0116261
```

Pinecone ranks results with BM25. Because the join reads the table with your own privileges, it respects row-level security and drops any row deleted since the last sync.

## Filter results

Use `filter` to restrict results by metadata columns, and `must` to require text in a column:

```sql SQL theme={null}
-- Only articles in the account category
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'settings',
       filter => '{"category": {"$eq": "account"}}', k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;

-- Only articles whose body contains the exact error code
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'import error',
       must => '{"body": {"$match_phrase": "E-1042"}}', k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

`must` accepts `$match_phrase`, `$match_all`, and `$match_any`. For the operators `filter` accepts, see [Filter operators](/guides/search/full-text-search#filter-operators).

To write the whole query in [Lucene syntax](/guides/search/full-text-search/query-syntax), set `mode => 'query_string'`:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'title:(password OR invoices) -body:email',
       mode => 'query_string', k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

## Combine text and vector search

If you declared a `vector_column`, pass a query vector with `vector`, and name the column the text query must match with `field`. The text query narrows the results to rows that match it in that column, and the vector ranks what's left:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'billing', field => 'body',
       vector => pinecone.embed('how do I get a receipt for my payment'), k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

```text Output theme={null}
 id |          title
----+--------------------------
  6 | Download past invoices
  5 | Change your billing plan
```

## Search one tenant

To keep each tenant's documents in their own Pinecone [namespace](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#namespaces), pass a tenant column as `partition_column` when you call `pinecone.track_docs()`. Then name the tenant with `partition` on every search. This example uses a `tickets` table with a `tenant_id` column:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.track_docs('tickets',
    text_columns     => '["title", "body"]',
    partition_column => 'tenant_id');

SELECT s.id, s.score
FROM pinecone.search_docs('tickets', 'invoice pdf', partition => 42, k => 10) s;
```

A search covers exactly one tenant, and BM25 scores are calculated within that tenant's documents. A search without `partition` returns an error. With [`engine => 'local'`](#search-without-pinecone), `partition` becomes a condition on the column instead. `pinecone.delete_partition('tickets', 42)` deletes one tenant's documents from Pinecone, and its rows stay in the table.

The partition column must be `NOT NULL`. Pinecone limits the number of namespaces per index by plan, and pg\_pinecone warns when a table has more than 1,000 distinct values.

## Highlight matches

`pinecone.headline()` marks the query terms in a column's text, using the language you declared for that column:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT a.id, pinecone.headline('articles', 'body', a.body, 'download invoice pdf') AS snippet
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'download invoice pdf', k => 2) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

```text Output theme={null}
 id |                                               snippet
----+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  6 | Every <b>invoice</b> is available as a <b>PDF</b> on the Billing page under <b>Invoice</b> history.
  3 | Go to Settings and choose Export to <b>download</b> every project as a CSV file.
```

## Search without Pinecone

Set `engine => 'local'` to answer the same call with Postgres's built-in full-text search instead of Pinecone:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT a.id, a.title, s.score
FROM pinecone.search_docs('articles', 'download invoice', engine => 'local', k => 3) s
JOIN articles a ON a.id = s.id::bigint
ORDER BY s.rank;
```

The local engine reflects writes immediately. It also works on tables you haven't declared with `track_docs()` if you name a column with `field`. It ranks results with Postgres's `ts_rank_cd` instead of BM25 and requires every query word to match, so it can return fewer results than the remote engine, in a different order. It doesn't support `filter`, `must`, `vector`, or `mode => 'query_string'`, and it doesn't create an index, so add a [GIN index](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-indexes.html) on large tables.

## Manage a tracked table

Once a table is tracked, pg\_pinecone keeps its Pinecone index in sync on its own. These functions handle the cases that need your attention:

* **Retry rejected documents**: If Pinecone rejects a document, pg\_pinecone sets it aside without stopping the rest of the table. `pinecone.failed_docs('articles')` lists rejected documents and why, and `pinecone.retry_failed_docs('articles')` queues them again.
* **Re-send every row**: `pinecone.backfill_docs('articles', clear => true)` copies the whole table again, for example after restoring a database backup.
* **Change a declared column**: Stop tracking the table before you drop, rename, or change the type of a declared column.
* **Stop tracking**: `pinecone.untrack_docs('articles', drop_index => true)` stops syncing and deletes the Pinecone index.

## Search an index directly

To work with a Pinecone index for full-text search that isn't tied to a table, use `pinecone.create_doc_index()`, `pinecone.upsert_docs()`, and `pinecone.search_doc_index()`:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.create_doc_index('faq',
  '{"fields": {"question": {"type": "string", "full_text_search": {"language": "en"}}}}');

SELECT pinecone.upsert_docs('faq',
  '[{"_id": "q1", "question": "How do I cancel my subscription?"},
    {"_id": "q2", "question": "Where can I find my invoices?"}]');

SELECT id, score
FROM pinecone.search_doc_index('faq',
  '{"type": "text", "fields": ["question"], "query": "invoices"}', k => 3);
```

Upserted documents become searchable shortly after Pinecone indexes them, so a search run immediately after an upsert may return nothing. The schema and query use the same JSON as the [Documents API](/guides/search/full-text-search).

To delete the index when you're done:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.drop_doc_index('faq');
```


# pg_pinecone
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/overview

pg_pinecone is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that runs the search engine Pinecone uses at scale inside Postgres, or on an index in Pinecone's cloud.

pg\_pinecone is an open-source PostgreSQL extension, licensed under [Apache 2.0](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/blob/main/LICENSE), that brings Pinecone's vector search into the Postgres database you already run. It runs on PostgreSQL 17 and 18 servers you manage yourself, because installing it needs superuser access. The `remote` engine and full-text search also need a server setting.

> [card] [Quickstart](/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart)
>
> Install the extension and search a table with a native index.

> [card] [Storage engines](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines)
>
> The pgvector, native, and remote engines, and when to use each.

> [card] [Switch from pgvector to native](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector)
>
> Replace a table's pgvector index with a native index.

> [card] [Switch from native to remote](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote)
>
> Switch a table to the remote engine when it outgrows one server.

## How it works

pg\_pinecone has three engines for a table's vector search:

* **`pgvector`**: Uses pgvector's own index, the same one you'd run without pg\_pinecone.
* **`native`**: The default. Runs the search engine Pinecone uses at scale, inside your Postgres database. It doesn't call Pinecone.
* **`remote`**: Runs the search on an index in Pinecone's cloud instead, for a table that outgrows one server.

Your tables and queries stay the same on every engine, and you switch a table between `native` and `remote` with one SQL call. Every switch can be reversed. Postgres keeps every row on every engine, including `remote`, so switching back rebuilds an index from data already in your database.

### Architecture

![An application sends pgvector SQL to Postgres, which keeps the rows and their vector column. pg\_pinecone searches them with the native engine (the default), the pgvector engine, or the remote engine, which syncs to a Pinecone serverless index and returns the results.](https://mintcdn.com/pinecone/qIfhVY6y5p5rJ02f/images/pg-pinecone/pg-pinecone-overview-light.svg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=qIfhVY6y5p5rJ02f\&q=85\&s=a925c57ae6c04da11de0bda31fb8041a)

The diagram names these index types:

* **HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): A graph index in pgvector. Each vector links to its nearest neighbors, and a search follows those links toward the query.
* **IVFFlat**: A clustered index in pgvector. It groups vectors into lists and compares the query with the full vectors in the lists nearest to it.
* **IVF + RaBitQ**: How the `native` engine searches. IVF (inverted file) groups vectors into clusters the same way, and RaBitQ stores each vector as a short binary code, so the index is small and quick to scan. The closest matches are then rechecked against the full vectors.

## Features

* **Filtered search**: With a [filter column](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines#filter-column), the `native` engine applies a filter, such as a tenant ID, during the search, so filtered queries return a full set of results. It runs in your database without an account or network access.
* **Scale**: The `remote` engine moves a table's vector search to a Pinecone index, and Postgres keeps the rows.
* **Unchanged queries**: A pgvector query like `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1` works the same on every engine.
* **Tenant isolation**: With the `remote` engine, each tenant can have its own Pinecone namespace, so a query searches only that tenant's data.
* **Full-text search**: pg\_pinecone keeps a Pinecone index for full-text search in sync with a table's text columns, and you run BM25, vector, or hybrid searches on it from SQL.
* **SQL functions**: You can generate embeddings and rerank results in SQL. See the [SQL reference](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/blob/main/docs/reference.md).

## Choose your path

* **New to vector search**: The [quickstart](/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart) creates a table with embeddings and searches it with a `native` index.
* **Already using pgvector**: [Switch from pgvector to native](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector).
* **Outgrowing one server**: [Switch from native to remote](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote), so Pinecone serves the table's vector search.
* **Leaving Postgres**: [Migrate from pgvector](/guides/index-data/migrate-from-pgvector) moves your data into Pinecone Database.


# pg_pinecone quickstart
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart

Install the pg_pinecone extension for Postgres and search a sample table with a native index, which runs the search engine Pinecone uses at scale.

This quickstart installs pg\_pinecone on a PostgreSQL server you manage. You create a sample table with vectors and search it with a `native` index, which runs the search engine Pinecone uses at scale inside Postgres. You can bring your own vectors, with no API key or network access, or have Pinecone generate embeddings. To compare `native` with the other engines, see [Storage engines](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines).

If you already have a table with a pgvector index, complete steps 1 and 2 to install pg\_pinecone, then [switch from pgvector to native](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector).

## Prerequisites

* A PostgreSQL 17 or 18 server and a superuser role on it.
* pgvector installed on that server, because pg\_pinecone uses its `vector` column type and distance operators. If you don't have it, run `sudo apt install postgresql-17-pgvector` on Debian or Ubuntu, or `brew install pgvector` with Homebrew on macOS. For other Linux distributions, see the [pgvector installation guide](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#installation). If you install with Docker, the image includes Postgres and pgvector, so you need only Docker.
* Optional: a [Pinecone API key](https://app.pinecone.io/organizations/-/projects/-/keys), if you want Pinecone to generate the embeddings. A key from the free [Starter plan](https://www.pinecone.io/pricing/) is enough.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `native` engine never calls Pinecone. Steps 3 and 4 each have two tabs, so pick the same one in both. **Your own vectors** runs entirely in your database with no API key or network access, and **Pinecone embeddings** generates embeddings with a Pinecone-hosted model.

## 1. Install pg\_pinecone

> [tab] Release archive
>
> 1. Download the release archive for your platform and Postgres version from the [releases page](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/releases).
>
>    Archives are published for PostgreSQL 17 and 18 on Linux x86\_64, Linux arm64, and macOS arm64. The Linux x86\_64 build needs a CPU that supports x86-64-v3 (Intel Haswell or newer, which covers current cloud instances), and the Linux builds need glibc 2.39 or later, such as Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 13.
>
> 2. Extract the archive and copy its files into your Postgres installation.
>
>    The commands use `PG=17`. If your server runs PostgreSQL 18, change it to `PG=18`. To check your version, run `pg_config --version`. `pg_config` also reports where your Postgres installation keeps extension files:
>
>    ```bash Linux theme={null}
>    PG=17
>    tar xzf pg_pinecone-0.11.0-pg$PG-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
>    sudo cp usr/lib/postgresql/$PG/lib/pg_pinecone.so "$(pg_config --pkglibdir)/"
>    sudo cp usr/share/postgresql/$PG/extension/pg_pinecone* "$(pg_config --sharedir)/extension/"
>    ```
>
>    ```bash macOS theme={null}
>    PG=17
>    tar xzf pg_pinecone-0.11.0-pg$PG-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
>    cp opt/homebrew/lib/postgresql@$PG/pg_pinecone.dylib "$(pg_config --pkglibdir)/"
>    cp opt/homebrew/share/postgresql@$PG/extension/pg_pinecone* "$(pg_config --sharedir)/extension/"
>    ```
>
> On Linux arm64, use the `linux-arm64` archive. If more than one Postgres version is installed, use the `pg_config` that belongs to the server you're installing into. On other platforms, including Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL 9, and older x86\_64 CPUs, [build from source](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone#readme).

> [tab] Docker
>
> The [`pineconeteam/pg_pinecone`](https://hub.docker.com/r/pineconeteam/pg_pinecone) image is the [`pgvector/pgvector`](https://hub.docker.com/r/pgvector/pgvector) image with pg\_pinecone added, so it includes Postgres and pgvector. It runs on x86\_64 and arm64 hosts. On x86\_64, it needs a CPU that supports x86-64-v3, like the Linux x86\_64 release archive.
>
> 1. Pull the image. The image includes its own Postgres, so you don't need to match a server you already have. This command uses PostgreSQL 17, the more widely used of the two supported versions. For PostgreSQL 18, use the `0.11.0-pg18` tag here and in the next step instead:
>
>    ```bash theme={null}
>    docker pull pineconeteam/pg_pinecone:0.11.0-pg17
>    ```
>
> 2. Start a container from the image:
>
>    ```bash theme={null}
>    docker run -d --name pg_pinecone \
>      -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
>      pineconeteam/pg_pinecone:0.11.0-pg17 \
>      -c shared_preload_libraries=pg_pinecone
>    ```
>
>    The `shared_preload_libraries` setting isn't needed for this quickstart, but the `remote` engine and full-text search need it, and setting it now saves a restart later.

## 2. Connect and create the extensions

1. Connect to your database as a superuser with `psql`:

   ```bash Linux theme={null}
   sudo -u postgres psql
   ```

   ```bash macOS theme={null}
   psql postgres
   ```

   ```bash Docker theme={null}
   docker exec -it pg_pinecone psql -U postgres
   ```

   On Linux, the `postgres` system user is the superuser that the package creates. With Homebrew on macOS, your own user is the superuser. In the Docker image, the superuser is `postgres`. To connect to a different database or a remote server, add `-d your_database`, `-h your_host`, and `-U your_superuser`.

2. Create the extensions. Create pgvector first, because pg\_pinecone builds on its `vector` type and operators:

   ```sql SQL theme={null}
   CREATE EXTENSION vector;
   CREATE EXTENSION pg_pinecone;
   ```

## 3. Add sample data

> [tab] Your own vectors
>
> 1. Create the table. These vectors have three dimensions:
>
>    ```sql SQL theme={null}
>    CREATE TABLE docs (
>        id        bigint PRIMARY KEY,
>        body      text,
>        embedding vector(3)
>    );
>    ```
>
> 2. Insert a few short documents with their vectors. In a real application, you'd generate the vectors with an embedding model of your choice. To skip that step here, each document gets a hand-made vector whose values stand for food, nature, and places:
>
>    ```sql SQL theme={null}
>    INSERT INTO docs (id, body, embedding) VALUES
>        (1, 'The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the World''s Fair in Paris.', '[0.1, 0.1, 0.9]'),
>        (2, 'Photosynthesis converts sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose.', '[0.05, 0.9, 0.1]'),
>        (3, 'The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system in the world.', '[0.1, 0.8, 0.3]'),
>        (4, 'Espresso is brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee.', '[0.95, 0.05, 0.05]'),
>        (5, 'Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and China.', '[0.05, 0.4, 0.8]'),
>        (6, 'Honeybees communicate the location of flowers with a waggle dance.', '[0.2, 0.85, 0.05]'),
>        (7, 'A croissant is a flaky pastry made from laminated, buttered dough.', '[0.95, 0.05, 0.1]'),
>        (8, 'The Amazon rainforest produces a large share of the world''s oxygen.', '[0.05, 0.9, 0.3]');
>    ```

> [tab] Pinecone embeddings
>
> 1. Store your Pinecone API key so the extension can generate embeddings. The key is stored in the `pinecone.secret` table, which only superusers can read by default:
>
>    ```sql SQL theme={null}
>    SELECT pinecone.set_api_key('YOUR_API_KEY');
>    ```
>
> 2. Create the table. The [`multilingual-e5-large`](/models/multilingual-e5-large) model that `pinecone.embed_batch()` uses by default produces 1024-dimensional vectors:
>
>    ```sql SQL theme={null}
>    CREATE TABLE docs (
>        id        bigint PRIMARY KEY,
>        body      text,
>        embedding vector(1024)
>    );
>    ```
>
> 3. Insert a few short documents and generate their embeddings in the same statement:
>
>    ```sql SQL theme={null}
>    WITH input(body) AS (
>        VALUES
>            ('The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the World''s Fair in Paris.'),
>            ('Photosynthesis converts sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose.'),
>            ('The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system in the world.'),
>            ('Espresso is brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee.'),
>            ('Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and China.'),
>            ('Honeybees communicate the location of flowers with a waggle dance.'),
>            ('A croissant is a flaky pastry made from laminated, buttered dough.'),
>            ('The Amazon rainforest produces a large share of the world''s oxygen.')
>    ),
>    numbered AS (
>        SELECT row_number() OVER () AS ordinal, body FROM input
>    )
>    INSERT INTO docs (id, body, embedding)
>    SELECT n.ordinal, n.body, e.embedding::vector
>    FROM numbered n
>    JOIN pinecone.embed_batch((SELECT array_agg(body ORDER BY ordinal) FROM numbered)) e
>      ON e.ordinal = n.ordinal;
>    ```

## 4. Search inside Postgres

### 1. Create a native index

Create a `native` index on the vector column. `native` is the default engine, so `engine => 'native'` is optional:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.create_index('docs', 'embedding', engine => 'native');
```

With Pinecone embeddings, `pinecone.create_index()` prints an informational message, labeled `NOTICE`, that suggests `SET STORAGE PLAIN` on the vector column, which speeds up searches on large tables. You can ignore it for this sample.

### 2. Run a search

Search with an ordinary pgvector query, the same query you'd run without pg\_pinecone. `<=>` is pgvector's cosine distance operator:

> [tab] Your own vectors
>
> Query with `[1, 0, 0]`, a vector that points entirely toward food, with no nature or places:
>
> ```sql SQL theme={null}
> SET enable_seqscan = off;
>
> SELECT id, body
> FROM docs
> ORDER BY embedding <=> '[1, 0, 0]'
> LIMIT 2;
> ```
>
> The two closest documents are the two about food:
>
> ```text Output theme={null}
>  id |                                 body
> ----+-----------------------------------------------------------------------
>   4 | Espresso is brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee.
>   7 | A croissant is a flaky pastry made from laminated, buttered dough.
> ```

> [tab] Pinecone embeddings
>
> Query with a question, which `pinecone.embed()` turns into a vector:
>
> ```sql SQL theme={null}
> SET enable_seqscan = off;
>
> SELECT id, body
> FROM docs
> ORDER BY embedding <=> (SELECT pinecone.embed('What should I order for breakfast at a cafe?')::vector)
> LIMIT 2;
> ```
>
> `::vector` converts the embedding to pgvector's `vector` type. The subquery embeds the question once, before the search, so Postgres can use the index. If you call `pinecone.embed()` directly in `ORDER BY`, Postgres reads every row instead.
>
> The two closest documents are about espresso and croissants, even though neither one mentions breakfast or a cafe:
>
> ```text Output theme={null}
>  id |                                 body
> ----+-----------------------------------------------------------------------
>   4 | Espresso is brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee.
>   7 | A croissant is a flaky pastry made from laminated, buttered dough.
> ```

> [!NOTE]
>
> `SET enable_seqscan = off` makes Postgres use the index on this eight-row table. On a table this small, the planner would otherwise read every row directly, because that's cheaper than using any index. Once a table is large enough that reading every row costs more, the planner chooses the index on its own, and you don't need this setting. It lasts until you disconnect.

### 3. Check which index served the query

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan Postgres uses to run a query, including which index it reads. To confirm the `native` index served the search, check the plan:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SET enable_seqscan = off;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT id
FROM docs
ORDER BY embedding <=> (SELECT embedding FROM docs WHERE id = 4)
LIMIT 2;
```

The plan includes `Index Scan using docs_embedding_pinecone_idx`, the `native` index you created in step 4.1. If Postgres read every row instead, the plan would show `Seq Scan`.

## 5. Clean up

If you don't need the sample table anymore, delete it. `DROP TABLE` permanently deletes the table, its rows, and its indexes, including the `native` index. To try [switching from native to remote](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote) next, skip this step, because that guide uses the same table.

```sql SQL theme={null}
DROP TABLE docs;
```

## Next steps

* [Choose a storage engine](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines) for your workload.
* [Switch from pgvector to native](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector) on an existing table.
* [Switch from native to remote](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote) when a table outgrows one server.
* [Search a table with full-text search](/guides/pg-pinecone/full-text-search).


# pg_pinecone storage engines
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines

Learn how pg_pinecone's pgvector, native, and remote storage engines work, when to use each, and how to switch between them.

pg\_pinecone searches a table's vector column with one of three engines: `pgvector` or `native` inside Postgres, or `remote` on Pinecone. The engine is a setting on the table's one pg\_pinecone index, so you switch engines per table. Your queries are the same on all three, so you can change engines without touching application code:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT id, body FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10;
```

## The engines

| Engine | What it is | Where vectors are searched | Needs a Pinecone account |
| - | - | - | - |
| `pgvector` | pgvector's own index, such as HNSW. | In Postgres | No |
| `native` | The search engine Pinecone uses at scale, running inside Postgres. This is the default. | In Postgres | No |
| `remote` | A Pinecone Database index, kept in sync with your table. | In Pinecone | Yes |

If you create an index without choosing an engine, you get `native`. A pgvector index that a table already has stays in place until you replace it.

A `native` index built on fewer than 10,000 rows compares each query with every row. That's exact, but it slows down as the table grows, so create the index after you load your data, or rebuild it with `REINDEX` once the table is larger.

Postgres stays the system of record with every engine. Your rows, including the vector column, live in Postgres, and the engine only decides which index answers similarity queries.

## When to use each engine

* **`pgvector`**: A table that already has a pgvector index and doesn't filter its searches. You can keep that index and add pg\_pinecone without changing anything.
* **`native`**: Filtered search, especially when the rows that match a filter are clustered, such as per-tenant data queried with `WHERE tenant_id = $1`. The `native` engine scans by cluster, so it keeps finding matches where a graph index like pgvector's [HNSW](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#hnsw) can miss them. It runs without an account or network access.
* **`remote`**: A table that has outgrown a single Postgres server. Pinecone stores and searches the vectors, and Postgres keeps the rest of the row.

## Switching engines

You switch a table between `native` and `remote` with one call to `pinecone.set_engine()`, in either direction:

* **To `remote`**: pg\_pinecone creates a Pinecone index and copies the table's vectors to it in the background. Queries keep using the `native` index until the copy finishes, and new writes go to both, so reads and writes are never interrupted. In version 0.10.0 and later, a table of a million rows takes up to about an hour to copy at the default settings.
* **To `native`**: pg\_pinecone queues a rebuild of the `native` index and keeps serving queries from Pinecone until the rebuild starts. The rebuild blocks reads that use the index, and writes to the table, until it finishes. That usually takes seconds to a few minutes, depending on table size. After the rebuild, pg\_pinecone deletes the Pinecone index it created.

To switch a pgvector index you created with `CREATE INDEX` to `native`, create the `native` index with `pinecone.create_index()`, then drop the pgvector index. A pgvector index that `pinecone.create_index()` built switches with one call, `pinecone.set_engine('your_table', 'native')`. To switch from `native` back to `pgvector`, drop the `native` index and create the pgvector index again.

Every switch can be reversed, and none of them loses data. Postgres keeps every row, including the vector column, on every engine, so switching back rebuilds an index from the table.

[Switch from pgvector to native](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector) and [Switch from native to remote](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote) walk through each switch.

## Filtered and multi-tenant tables

An index can cover one extra column besides the vector, either as a filter column or as a partition column. Both apply to queries that include `WHERE column = value`.

### Filter column

A filter column narrows the search inside the index instead of after it. Set it with `filter_column` when you create a `native` or `remote` index:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.create_index('docs', 'embedding', engine => 'native', filter_column => 'tenant_id');

SELECT id, body FROM docs
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;
```

* **On `native`**: The engine applies the filter while it scans.
* **On `remote`**: pg\_pinecone stores the column as Pinecone metadata and sends `WHERE tenant_id = $1` to Pinecone as a [metadata filter](/guides/search/filter-by-metadata). A filtered `native` index keeps its filter column when you switch it to `remote`.
* **Other conditions**: Only `=` on the filter column is applied inside the index. Any other condition, such as a range or a second column, is applied to each batch the index returns, so a selective one can leave fewer rows than `LIMIT`. On `native`, the scan keeps going until the query has enough rows, because `pinecone.iterative_scan` defaults to `auto`. On `remote`, the scan asks Pinecone for more rows, up to 10,000, and returns an error if that's still not enough. To return the rows found instead, run `SET pinecone.iterative_scan = 'relaxed_order'`. Rows after the first batch arrive in batch order, so re-sort them if exact order matters. On the `pgvector` engine, use pgvector's own [`hnsw.iterative_scan`](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#iterative-index-scans) instead.

The filter column must be a `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint`, `text`, or `varchar` column.

### Partition column

A partition column gives each value its own Pinecone [namespace](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#namespaces), so each tenant's vectors are stored and searched separately. It applies to the `remote` engine:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.create_index('docs', 'embedding', engine => 'remote', partition_column => 'tenant_id');
```

* **Namespaces**: Each value maps to a namespace named `<schema>.<table>:<value>`, such as `public.docs:42`.
* **Queries**: Every query must include `WHERE tenant_id = <value>`, and it searches only that tenant's namespace. A query without it returns an error instead of searching across tenants.
* **Removing a tenant**: `pinecone.delete_partition('docs', 42)` deletes that tenant's namespace. Its rows stay in the table.
* **Limits**: The column must be `NOT NULL`. Pinecone limits the number of namespaces per index by plan, and pg\_pinecone warns when a table has more than 1,000 distinct values.

You can also set `partition_column` when you switch a filtered `native` index to `remote` with `pinecone.set_engine()`.

## Consistency with the remote engine

When a table uses the `remote` engine, each committed write is queued in Postgres and copied to Pinecone by a background worker, usually within a few seconds. Under heavy write load, the queue can fall behind, and new rows can take minutes to become searchable.

* **No read-your-writes**: A query run right after a write may not reflect it yet.
* **Rolled-back writes never reach Pinecone**: Only committed changes are queued.
* **Postgres keeps working if Pinecone is unreachable**: Writes still commit in Postgres, and the queue holds them and retries while Pinecone is unavailable.
* **Searches aren't retried**: If Pinecone rejects a search because of a rate limit or a server error, the query fails immediately. Retry with backoff in your application, or spread tenants across namespaces with a [partition column](#partition-column).

`pinecone.status()` lists each table that syncs to Pinecone, with its `mode` and how many writes are still queued (`backlog`). Tables on `native` don't appear. A table whose pgvector index `pinecone.create_index()` built appears with `mode` `local`. The [operator runbook](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/blob/main/docs/runbook.md) covers monitoring the queue and handling writes that Pinecone rejects.


# pg_pinecone support
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/support

Ask questions about pg_pinecone in the Pinecone Discord community, and report bugs or request features in GitHub issues.

* **Questions and feedback**: Ask in the [Pinecone Discord community](https://discord.gg/tJ8V62S3sH), where other users and the Pinecone team answer.
* **Bugs and feature requests**: Open an issue in the [pg\_pinecone repository](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/issues). To propose a code change, open an issue first so the approach can be agreed on before any work starts.
* **Security issues**: Don't open a public issue. Email [security@pinecone.io](mailto:security@pinecone.io), or follow the [security policy](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pg_pinecone/blob/main/SECURITY.md) to report it privately on GitHub.
* **Your Pinecone account or index**: For a problem with the Pinecone index that the `remote` engine or full-text search uses, [contact Pinecone Support](/admin/support/contact-support).

When you report a bug, include your pg\_pinecone and Postgres versions, your operating system, the table's engine, and the full error message. To find the versions, run:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_pinecone';
SELECT version();
```


# Switch from pgvector to native
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-from-pgvector

Replace a table's pgvector index with a pg_pinecone native index without changing your queries, and switch back to pgvector if you need to.

A table with a pgvector index, such as an [HNSW index](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#hnsw), is on the `pgvector` engine. You can switch it to `native`, which runs the search engine Pinecone uses at scale inside Postgres. Your queries and data stay the same, and you can [switch back to pgvector](#switch-back-to-pgvector) at any time.

## Before you begin

* pg\_pinecone installed and created in the database, as steps 1 and 2 of the [quickstart](/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart) show.
* A table with a `vector` column and a pgvector index on that column created with `CREATE INDEX`. If `pinecone.create_index()` built the pgvector index instead, skip this guide and switch it with one call: `SELECT pinecone.set_engine('your_table', 'native');`.
* A single-column primary key, if you plan to [switch to `remote`](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote) later. A `native` index doesn't need one.

## Replace the index

### 1. Create a native index

Create a `native` index on the table's `vector` column. The pgvector index keeps serving queries while the `native` index builds:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.create_index('your_table', 'embedding', engine => 'native');
```

`pinecone.create_index()` uses cosine distance by default. If your pgvector index uses a different distance, pass the matching `metric`: `'l2'` for `vector_l2_ops`, or `'ip'` for `vector_ip_ops`.

If your queries filter on one column, such as a tenant ID, add it as a filter column with `filter_column => 'tenant_id'`. See [Filter column](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines#filter-column).

### 2. Drop the pgvector index

```sql SQL theme={null}
DROP INDEX your_hnsw_index;
```

Your queries now use the `native` index.

### 3. Check which index serves queries

Run `EXPLAIN` on a similarity query. This one uses a row's own vector as the query:

```sql SQL theme={null}
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM your_table
ORDER BY embedding <=> (SELECT embedding FROM your_table LIMIT 1)
LIMIT 10;
```

The plan includes `Index Scan using your_table_embedding_pinecone_idx`. `pinecone.create_index()` names the index `<table>_<column>_pinecone_idx`. On a small table, Postgres may choose to read every row instead of using any index, because that's cheaper.

## Switch back to pgvector

If the table uses the `remote` engine, [switch it back to `native`](/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote#switch-back-to-native) first.

### 1. Drop the native index

```sql SQL theme={null}
DROP INDEX your_table_embedding_pinecone_idx;
```

Until the pgvector index exists, queries on the table read every row.

### 2. Create the pgvector index

```sql SQL theme={null}
CREATE INDEX your_hnsw_index ON your_table USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```

Postgres builds the index from the vectors already in the table.


# Switch from native to remote
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/pg-pinecone/switch-to-remote

Switch a pg_pinecone table from the native engine to the remote engine, so Pinecone serves its vector search while Postgres keeps the rows.

When a table outgrows a single Postgres server, you can move its vector search to Pinecone by switching the table to the `remote` engine. Pinecone stores a copy of the vectors and answers the table's similarity queries, and Postgres keeps every row. Your queries don't change, and you can [switch back to native](#switch-back-to-native) at any time.

## Before you begin

* pg\_pinecone installed, as the [quickstart](/guides/pg-pinecone/quickstart) shows.
* A Pinecone API key stored in the database, which the `remote` engine needs even if you bring your own vectors. Store it with `SELECT pinecone.set_api_key('YOUR_API_KEY');`.
* A table with a `native` index. The examples use the `docs` table from the quickstart, so skip the quickstart's clean-up step if you want to follow along.

## Switch to the remote engine

The `remote` engine relies on a background worker that copies writes to Pinecone, and Postgres starts that worker only when the extension is preloaded.

### 1. Preload the extension

Add `pg_pinecone` to `shared_preload_libraries` in `postgresql.conf`. To find the file, run `SHOW config_file;` in `psql`. If the setting already lists other libraries, add `pg_pinecone` to the list:

```ini postgresql.conf theme={null}
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_pinecone'
```

Then restart Postgres. For example, `sudo systemctl restart postgresql` on most Linux installs, or `brew services restart postgresql@17` with Homebrew on macOS.

### 2. Switch the engine

Reconnect and switch the table to the `remote` engine:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.set_engine('docs', 'remote');
```

This creates a serverless index in your Pinecone project and starts copying the table's vectors to it in the background. The index is created in `aws` `us-east-1` unless you set `pinecone.am_cloud` and `pinecone.am_region` first. While the copy runs, queries keep using the `native` index, so reads and writes aren't interrupted.

### 3. Wait for the copy to finish

Check progress with `pinecone.status()`:

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT table_name, mode, index_name, backlog FROM pinecone.status();
```

`mode` is `promoting` while the copy runs. When `mode` is `remote` and `backlog` is `0`, Pinecone is serving the table's queries. In version 0.10.0 and later, a table of a million rows takes up to about an hour to copy at the default settings.

### 4. Run the same query

Run the quickstart's query again, unchanged:

> [tab] Your own vectors
>
> ```sql SQL theme={null}
> SET enable_seqscan = off;
>
> SELECT id, body
> FROM docs
> ORDER BY embedding <=> '[1, 0, 0]'
> LIMIT 2;
> ```

> [tab] Pinecone embeddings
>
> ```sql SQL theme={null}
> SET enable_seqscan = off;
>
> SELECT id, body
> FROM docs
> ORDER BY embedding <=> (SELECT pinecone.embed('What should I order for breakfast at a cafe?')::vector)
> LIMIT 2;
> ```

Pinecone now serves the results. The new index also appears in the [Pinecone console](https://app.pinecone.io/organizations/-/projects/-/indexes) under the name `pinecone.status()` reports.

New writes to the table reach Pinecone within a few seconds, so a query run immediately after a write may not reflect it yet. See [Consistency with the remote engine](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines#consistency-with-the-remote-engine) for details.

## Switch back to native

Switching back moves the table's search into Postgres again. Postgres still has every row, so nothing is copied back from Pinecone. The rebuild blocks queries and writes on the table while it runs, as [Switching engines](/guides/pg-pinecone/storage-engines#switching-engines) explains, so plan it for a quiet period.

### 1. Switch the engine back

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT pinecone.set_engine('docs', 'native');
```

pg\_pinecone rebuilds the `native` index from the table, then deletes the Pinecone index it created.

### 2. Check that the switch finished

```sql SQL theme={null}
SELECT table_name, mode FROM pinecone.status();
```

The table is back on `native` when it no longer appears in the results. The rebuild runs in the background, so the table can still show `remote` for a few seconds on a small table, or longer on a large one.

## Query the index from your application

The Pinecone index that the `remote` engine creates is a standard [Pinecone Database](/guides/get-started/overview) index, so your application can also query it directly with a [Pinecone SDK](/reference/sdks/python/overview). The table's records are in a namespace named after the table, such as `public.docs`, so pass that namespace in your query. Its record IDs are Postgres row locations in `block:offset` form, not your primary key values, so look up matching rows through Postgres. To move a workload off Postgres entirely, see [Migrate from pgvector](/guides/index-data/migrate-from-pgvector).

# Pinecone 2022 changelog
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/release-notes/2022

Every change to Pinecone in 2022, including new features, API updates, deprecations, and pricing and plan changes.

All Pinecone products share this changelog. Use the filters to narrow the list.

**2022-12-22**

### Pinecone is now available in Google Cloud Marketplace

You can now [sign up for Pinecone billing through Google Cloud Marketplace](/admin/billing/upgrade-billing-plan).

**2022-12-06**

### Organizations are generally available

Pinecone now features [organizations](/admin/organizations/understanding-organizations), which allow one or more users to control billing and project settings across multiple projects owned by the same organization.

**2022-12-06**

### p2 pod type is generally available

The [p2 pod type](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#p2-pods) is now generally available and ready for production workloads. p2 pods are now available in the Starter plan and support the [dotproduct distance metric](/guides/index-data/create-an-index#dotproduct).

**2022-12-06**

### Performance improvements

* [Bulk vector deletes](/guides/index-data/upsert-data/#deleting-vectors) are now up to 10x faster in many circumstances.
* [Creating collections](/guides/manage-data/back-up-an-index) is now faster.

**2022-10-31**

### Hybrid search is in early access

Pinecone now supports keyword-aware semantic search with the new hybrid search indexes and endpoints. Hybrid search enables improved relevance for semantic search results by combining them with keyword search.

This is an **early access** feature and is available only by [signing up](https://www.pinecone.io/hybrid-search-early-access/).

**2022-10-17**

### Status page

The new [Pinecone Status Page](https://status.pinecone.io/) displays information about the status of the Pinecone service, including the status of individual cloud regions and a log of recent incidents.

**2022-09-16**

### Public collections

You can now create indexes from public collections, which are collections containing public data from real-world data sources. Currently, public collections include the Glue - SSTB collection, the TREC Question classification collection, and the SQuAD collection.

**2022-08-16**

### Collections are in public preview

You can now [make static copies of your index using collections](/guides/manage-data/back-up-an-index). After you create a collection from an index, you can create a new index from that collection. The new index can use any pod type and any number of pods. Collections only consume storage.

This is a **public preview** feature and isn't appropriate for production workloads.

**2022-08-16**

### Vertical scaling

You can now [change the size of the pods](/guides/indexes/pods/scale-pod-based-indexes#increase-pod-size) for a live index to accommodate more vectors or queries without interrupting reads or writes. The p1 and s1 pod types are now available in [4 different sizes](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview/#pods-pod-types-and-pod-sizes): `1x`, `2x`, `4x`, and `8x`. Capacity and compute per pod double with each size increment.

**2022-08-16**

### p2 pod type is in public preview

The new [p2 pod type](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview/#p2-pods) provides search speeds of around 5ms and throughput of 200 queries per second per replica, or approximately 10x faster speeds and higher throughput than the p1 pod type, depending on your data and network conditions.

This is a **public preview** feature and isn't appropriate for production workloads.

**2022-08-16**

### Improved p1 and s1 performance

The [s1](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview/#s1-pods) and [p1](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview/#p1-pods) pod types now offer approximately 50% higher query throughput and 50% lower latency, depending on your workload.

**2022-07-26**

### Metadata filtering for `describe_index_stats`

You can now specify a [metadata filter](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#metadata) to get results for a subset of the vectors in your index by calling [`describe_index_stats`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/describe_index) with a [filter](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/describe_index#!path=filter\&t=request) object.

The `describe_index_stats` operation now uses the `POST` HTTP request type. The `filter` parameter is only accepted by `describe_index_stats` calls using the `POST` request type. Calls to `describe_index_stats` using the `GET` request type are now deprecated.

**2022-07-12**

### Pinecone console guided tour

You can now choose to follow a guided tour in the [Pinecone console](https://app.pinecone.io). This interactive tutorial walks you through creating your first index, upserting vectors, and querying your data. The purpose of the tour is to show you all the steps you need to start your first project in Pinecone.

**2022-06-24**

### Updated response codes

The [`create_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/create_index), [`delete_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/delete_index), and `scale_index` operations now use more specific HTTP response codes that describe the type of operation that succeeded.

**2022-06-07**

### Selective metadata indexing

You can now store more metadata and more unique metadata values. [Select which metadata fields you want to index for filtering](/guides/indexes/pods/manage-pod-based-indexes#selective-metadata-indexing) and which fields you only wish to store and retrieve. When you index metadata fields, you can filter vector search queries using those fields. When you store metadata fields without indexing them, you keep memory utilization low, especially when you have many unique metadata values, and therefore can fit more vectors per pod.

**2022-06-07**

### Single-vector queries

You can now [specify a single query vector using the vector input](/reference/api/2024-07/data-plane/query/#!path=vector\&t=request). We now encourage all users to query using a single vector rather than a batch of vectors, because batching queries can lead to long response messages and query times, and single queries execute just as fast on the server side.

**2022-06-07**

### Query by ID

You can now [query your Pinecone index using only the ID for another vector](/reference/api/2024-07/data-plane/query/#!path=id\&t=request). This is useful when you want to search for the nearest neighbors of a vector that's already stored in Pinecone.

**2022-06-07**

### Improved index fullness accuracy

The index fullness metric in [`describe_index_stats`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/describe_index#!c=200\&path=indexFullness\&t=response) results is now more accurate.

**2022-04-25**

### Partial updates are in public preview

You can now perform a partial update by ID and individual value pairs. This allows you to update individual metadata fields without having to upsert a matching vector or update all metadata fields at once.

**2022-04-25**

### New metrics

Users on all plans can now see metrics for the past one (1) week in the Pinecone console. Users on the Enterprise plan now have access to the following metrics via the [Prometheus metrics endpoint](/guides/production/monitoring/):

* `pinecone_vector_count`
* `pinecone_request_count_total`
* `pinecone_request_error_count_total`
* `pinecone_request_latency_seconds`
* `pinecone_index_fullness` (public preview)

The accuracy of the `pinecone_index_fullness` metric is improved. This may result in changes from historic reported values. This metric is in public preview.

**2022-04-25**

### Spark connector

Spark users who want to manage parallel upserts into Pinecone can now use the [official Spark connector for Pinecone](https://github.com/pinecone-io/spark-pinecone#readme) to upsert their data from a Spark dataframe.

**2022-04-25**

### Support for Boolean and float metadata in Pinecone indexes

You can now add `Boolean` and `float64` values to [metadata JSON objects associated with a Pinecone index](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#metadata).

**2022-04-25**

### New state field in `describe_index` results

The [`describe_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/describe_index/) operation results now contain a value for `state`, which describes the state of the index. The possible values for `state` are `Initializing`, `ScalingUp`, `ScalingDown`, `Terminating`, and `Ready`.

**2022-04-25**

### Delete by metadata filter

The [Delete](/reference/api/2024-07/data-plane/delete/) operation now supports filtering by metadata.

Released [`v5.4.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-python-client/releases/tag/v5.4.0) and [`v5.4.1`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-python-client/releases/tag/v5.4.1) of the [Pinecone Python SDK](/reference/sdks/python/overview). `v5.4.0` adds a `query_namespaces` utility method to [run a query in parallel across multiple namespaces](/reference/sdks/python/overview#query-across-namespaces) in an index and then merge the result sets into a single ranked result set with the `top_k` most relevant results. `v5.4.1` adds support for the `pinecone-plugin-inference` package required for some [integrated inference](/reference/api/introduction#inference) operations.

This version uses the latest stable API version, `2024-10`, and adds support for [reranking](/guides/search/rerank-results) and [import](/guides/index-data/import-data).

This version uses the latest stable API version, `2024-10`, and adds support for [embedding](/reference/api/2025-01/inference/generate-embeddings), [reranking](/reference/api/2025-01/inference/rerank), and [import](/guides/index-data/import-data).

> [!WARNING]
>
> `v3.0.0` also includes the following [breaking change](/reference/api/versioning#breaking-changes): The `control` class has been renamed `db_control`. Before upgrading to this version, be sure to update all relevant `import` statements to account for this change.
>
> For example, you would change `import org.openapitools.control.client.model.*;` to `import org.openapitools.db_control.client.model.*;`.

`v5.3.0` and `v5.3.1` of the [Pinecone Python SDK](/reference/sdks/python/overview) use the latest stable API version, `2024-10`. These versions were release previously.

This version depends on Pinecone API version `2024-07` and includes the ability to [prevent accidental index deletion](/guides/manage-data/manage-indexes#configure-deletion-protection). Additionally, this version includes the following **breaking changes**:

* `createServerlessIndex()` now requires a new argument: `DeletionProtection.ENABLED` or `DeletionProtection.DISABLED`.
* `configureIndex()` has been renamed `configurePodsIndex()`.

For more details, see the [Java SDK v2.0.0 migration guide](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-java-client/blob/main/v2-migration.md).

**2024-07-19**

Released version `2024-07` of the [Database API](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/list_indexes) and Inference API. This version includes the following highlights:

* The [`create_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/create_index) and [`configure_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/configure_index) endpoints now support the `deletion_protection` parameter. Setting this parameter to `"enabled"` prevents an index from accidental deletion. For more details, see [Prevent index deletion](/guides/manage-data/manage-indexes#configure-deletion-protection).

* The [`describe_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/describe_index) and [`list_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/list_indexes) responses now include the `deletion_protection` field. This field indicates whether deletion protection is enabled for an index.

* The `spec.serverless.cloud` and `spec.serverless.region` parameters of [`create_index`](/reference/api/2024-07/control-plane/create_index) now support `gcp` / `us-central` and `azure` / `eastus2` as part of the serverless public preview on GCP and Azure.

**2024-04-22**

As announced in January 2024, [control plane](/guides/core-concepts/architecture#control-plane) operations like `create_index`, `describe_index`, and `list_indexes` now use a single global URL, `https://api.pinecone.io`, regardless of the cloud environment where an index is hosted. This is now in general availability. As a result, the legacy version of the API, which required regional URLs for control plane operations, is deprecated as of April 15, 2024 and will be removed in a future, to be announced, release.

**2024-01-09**

The latest versions of Pinecone's Python SDK (v3.0.0) and Node.js SDK (v2.0.0) support the new API. To use the new API, existing users must upgrade to the new client versions and adapt some code. For guidance, see the [Python SDK v3 migration guide](https://canyon-quilt-082.notion.site/Pinecone-Python-SDK-v3-0-0-Migration-Guide-056d3897d7634bf7be399676a4757c7b) and [Node.js SDK v2 migration guide](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-ts-client/blob/main/v2-migration.md).

**2024-01-09**

The Pinecone documentation is now versioned. The default "latest" version reflects the new Pinecone API. The "legacy" version reflects the previous API, which requires regional URLs for control plane operations and doesn't support serverless indexes.

**2024-01-09**

The [new Pinecone API](/reference/api) gives you the same great vector database but with a drastically improved developer experience. The most significant improvements include:

* [Serverless indexes](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview): With serverless indexes, you don't configure or manage compute and storage resources. You just load your data and your indexes scale automatically based on usage. Likewise, you don't pay for dedicated resources that may sometimes lay idle. Instead, the pricing model for serverless indexes is consumption-based: You pay only for the amount of data stored and operations performed, with no minimums.

* [Multi-region projects](/admin/projects/understanding-projects): Instead of choosing a cloud region for an entire project, you now [choose a region for each index](/guides/index-data/create-an-index#create-a-serverless-index) in a project. This makes it possible to consolidate related indexes in the same project, even when they're hosted in different regions.

* [Global URL for control plane operations](/reference): Control plane operations like `create_index`, `describe_index`, and `list_indexes` now use a single global URL, `https://api.pinecone.io`, regardless of the cloud environment where an index is hosted. This simplifies the experience compared to the legacy API, where each environment has a unique URL.


# Pinecone 2025 changelog
Source: https://docs.pinecone.io/release-notes/2025

Every change to Pinecone in 2025, including new features, API updates, deprecations, and pricing and plan changes.

All Pinecone products share this changelog. Use the filters to narrow the list.

**2025-12-29**

### Increased metadata limit for assistants

The metadata field limit for assistants has been increased from 1KB to 16KB.

Assistant metadata is a JSON object that you can use to store custom organizational data, tags, and attributes for your assistants. You can specify metadata when creating an assistant by including a `metadata` field in your request, or update it later using the update assistant endpoint.

For more information, see [Create an assistant](/reference/api/latest/assistant/create_assistant) and [Manage assistants](/guides/assistant/manage-assistants).

**2025-12-23**

### Test Pinecone at scale

Added a new guide to help you [test Pinecone at production scale](/guides/optimize/test-at-scale). The guide describes how to create an index, import 10 million vectors, and then use Vector Search Bench (VSB) to capture performance metrics for 100,000 queries. To run this test, consider signing up for a [Standard plan trial](/admin/billing/standard-trial).

**2025-12-22**

### Pinecone Assistant now supports GPT-5

Pinecone Assistant now supports the GPT-5 model. To use it, set `model` to `gpt-5` when [chatting with your assistant](/reference/api/latest/assistant/chat_assistant).

For more information, see [Chat with Assistant](/guides/assistant/chat-with-assistant#choose-a-model) and [Chat through the OpenAI-compatible interface](/guides/assistant/chat-through-the-openai-compatible-interface#choose-a-model).

**2025-12-12**

### Upgrade from Starter to Standard trial

Organizations on the Starter plan can now upgrade to a Standard plan trial at any time. The Standard trial provides 21 days and \$300 in credits to test Pinecone at scale, with access to Standard plan features such as higher limits. For more information, see [Standard plan trial](/admin/billing/standard-trial).

**2025-12-07**

### Delete Assistant files while they are still processing

You can now delete a file uploaded to an assistant while it's still processing. Previously, you had to wait for file processing to complete before you could delete a file.

For more information, see [Manage files](/guides/assistant/manage-files).

**2025-12-02**

### Annual commit discount

In the Pinecone console, customers on Standard and Enterprise pay-as-you-go plans can now commit to an annual contract and receive a discount on usage. For more information, see [Understanding cost](/guides/manage-cost/understanding-cost#prepaid-credits).

**2025-12-02**

### Increased instructions limit for assistants

The maximum size for assistant instructions has been increased from 8 KB to 16 KB.

Instructions are included in every chat API call. Longer instructions increase input token costs for each request and consume more of the LLM's context window, reducing available space for retrieved context and conversation history.

For more information, see [Create an assistant](/reference/api/latest/assistant/create_assistant) and [Manage assistants](/guides/assistant/manage-assistants).

**2025-12-01**

### Dedicated Read Nodes: now in public preview

[Dedicated Read Nodes](/guides/index-data/dedicated-read-nodes/overview) is now in [public preview](/release-notes/feature-availability). Users on Standard and Enterprise plans can now create Dedicated Read Nodes indexes using the console and API.

With Dedicated Read Nodes, you can provision read hardware for large, high-throughput indexes that require predictable, low latency.

For more information, see [Dedicated Read Nodes](/guides/index-data/dedicated-read-nodes/overview).

**2025-11-19**

### Pinecone API version `2025-10` is now the latest stable version

`2025-10` is now the latest [stable version](/reference/api/versioning#release-schedule) of the [Pinecone APIs](/reference/api/introduction). This version doesn't include any breaking changes, and provides the following new features:

**[Dedicated read nodes](/guides/index-data/dedicated-read-nodes/overview) (early access):**

* The [Create an index](/reference/api/2025-10/control-plane/create_index) and [Configure index](/reference/api/2025-10/control-plane/configure_index) endpoints allow you to create and configure indexes that use dedicated read nodes. With dedicated read nodes, you can allocate dedicated hardware for read operations. This is useful for large, high-QPS indexes that require consistent, predictable low latency.
* The [Describe an index](/reference/api/2025-10/control-plane/describe_index) endpoint now allows you to view information about a dedicated index: shards, replicas, and scaling status.

**Namespace and metadata schema management:**

* The [Create a namespace](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/createnamespace) endpoint allows you to create a namespace without upserting vectors. You can optionally configure a metadata schema when creating the namespace to pre-declare which metadata fields should be indexed for filtering.
* The [List namespaces](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/listnamespaces) endpoint now supports filtering namespaces by prefix and returns the total count of matching namespaces.
* The [Describe a namespace](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/describenamespace) endpoint allows you to view the metadata schema configuration for a namespace, including which fields are indexed for filtering.
* The [Create an index](/reference/api/2025-10/control-plane/create_index) endpoint now allows you to specify a metadata schema at index creation time to pre-declare which metadata fields should be indexed for filtering across all namespaces.

**Update and fetch by metadata:**

* The [Update a vector](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/update) endpoint allows you to update metadata across multiple records in a namespace using a metadata filter expression, eliminating the need to update records individually by ID.
* The [Fetch vectors by metadata](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/fetch_by_metadata) endpoint allows you to fetch vectors using metadata filters without knowing their vector IDs.

**Enhanced sparse search:**

* The [Search with text](/reference/api/2025-10/data-plane/search_records) endpoint now supports a `match_terms` parameter that allows you to specify terms that must be present in search results for sparse indexes.

**2025-11-03**

### n8n quickstarts

Added new quickstart options to create an n8n workflow that downloads files via HTTP and lets you chat with them using Pinecone and OpenAI.

* [n8n quickstart for Pinecone Assistant](/guides/assistant/quickstart/n8n-quickstart)
* [n8n quickstart for Pinecone Database](/integrations/n8n)

**2025-11-03**

### Released Node.js SDK v6.1.3

Released [`v6.1.3`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-ts-client/releases/tag/v6.1.3) of the [Pinecone Node.js SDK](/reference/sdks/node/overview).

This version of the SDK fixes a bug in `Assistant.listFiles()`. Previously, when passing a `filter` to `listFiles`, the top-level `metadata` object wasn't handled correctly. This caused the method to return all files, regardless of the filter.

It's no longer necessary to provide a top-level `metadata` object. Instead, declare metadata fields directly in the `filter` object:

* ✅ `const files = await assistant.listFiles({ filter: { document_type: 'manuscript' } });`
* ❌ `const files = await assistant.listFiles({ filter: { metadata: { document_type: 'manuscript' } } });`

If you're using the old syntax, update it so that your filter works correctly. For more information about listing the files associated with an assistant, see [Manage files](/guides/assistant/manage-files).

**2025-10-30**

### Increased files per assistant on the Starter plan

On the Starter plan, you can now upload up to 100 files to an assistant. Previously, the limit was 10 files.

To learn more, see [Assistant limits](/guides/assistant/pricing-and-limits#assistant-limits).

**2025-10-23**

### Enhanced monthly spend alerts

You can now set multiple spend alerts to monitor your organization's monthly spending. These alerts notify designated recipients when spending reaches specified thresholds. The alerts automatically reset at the start of each monthly billing cycle.

Additionally, to protect from unexpected cost increases, Pinecone sends an alert when spending exceeds double your previous month's invoice amount. While the alert threshold is fixed, you can modify which email addresses receive the alert and enable or disable the alert notifications.

To learn more, see [Set monthly spend alerts](/guides/manage-cost/set-spend-alerts).

**2025-10-16**

### Agentic quickstart

Added new [agentic quickstart](/integrations/ai-coding-tools) options to help you build Pinecone applications with AI coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor. Instead of copying code snippets, you work with an agent that understands Pinecone APIs and implements production-ready patterns automatically.

**2025-08-12**

### Assistant MCP server endpoint update

**Breaking Change**: After August 31, 2025 at 11:59:59 PM UTC, the SSE-based MCP endpoint for assistants (`/mcp/assistants/<YOUR_ASSISTANT_NAME>/sse`) will no longer work.

Before then, update your applications to use the streamable HTTP transport MCP endpoint (`/mcp/assistants/<YOUR_ASSISTANT_NAME>`). This endpoint follows the current [MCP protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports#streamable-http) and provides improved flexibility and compatibility.

Assistant MCP servers are in [early access](/release-notes/feature-availability) and aren't intended for production usage.

For more information, see [Use an Assistant MCP server](/guides/assistant/mcp-server).

**2025-02-07**

### Released Python SDK v6.0.0

Released [`v6.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-python-client/releases/tag/v6.0.0) of the [Pinecone Python SDK](/reference/sdks/python/overview). This version uses the latest stable API version, `2025-01`, and includes support for the following:

* [Index tags](/guides/manage-data/manage-indexes#configure-index-tags) to categorize and identify your indexes.
* [Integrated inference](/reference/api/introduction#inference) without the need for extra plugins. If you were using the preview functionality of integrated inference, you must uninstall the `pinecone-plugin-records` package to use the `v6.0.0` release.
* Enum objects to help with the discoverability of some configuration options, for example, `Metric`, `AwsRegion`, `GcpRegion`, `PodType`, `EmbedModel`, `RerankModel`. This is a backwards compatible change; you can still pass string values for affected fields.
* New client variants, `PineconeAsyncio` and `IndexAsyncio`, which provide `async` methods for use with [asyncio](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html). This makes it possible to use Pinecone with modern async web frameworks such as [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/), [Quart](https://quart.palletsprojects.com/en/latest/), and [Sanic](https://sanic.dev/en/). Async support should significantly increase the efficiency of running many upserts in parallel.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Before upgrading to `v6.0.0`, update all relevant code to account for the following [breaking changes](/reference/api/versioning#breaking-changes). See the [`v6.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-python-client/releases/tag/v6.0.0) release notes for full details.
>
> * Incorporated the `pinecone-plugin-records` and `pinecone-plugin-inference` plugins into the `pinecone` package. If you are using these plugins, you must unstall them to use `v6.0.0`.
> * Dropped support for Python 3.8, which has now reached official end of life, and added support for Python 3.13.
> * Removed the explicit dependency on `tqdm`, which is used to provide a progress bar when upserting data into Pinecone. If `tqdm` is available in the environment, the Pinecone SDK will detect and use it, but `tdqm` is no longer required to run the SDK. Popular notebook platforms such as [Jupyter](https://jupyter.org/) and [Google Colab](https://colab.google/) already include `tqdm` in the environment by default, but if you are running small scripts in other environments and want to continue seeing progress bars, you will need to separately install the `tqdm` package.
> * Removed some previously deprecated and rarely used keyword arguments (`config`, `openapi_config`, and `index_api`) to instead prefer dedicated keyword arguments for individual settings such as `api_key`, `proxy_url`, etc.

**2025-02-07**

### Released Java SDK v4.0.0

Released [`v4.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-java-client/releases/tag/v4.0.0) of the [Pinecone Java SDK](/reference/sdks/java/overview). This version uses the latest stable API version, `2025-01`, and adds support for [sparse-only indexes](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#indexes-with-sparse-vectors).

> [!WARNING]
>
> Before upgrading to `v4.0.0`, update all relevant code to account for the following [breaking changes](/reference/api/versioning#breaking-changes). See the [`v4.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-java-client/releases/tag/v4.0.0) release notes for full details.
>
> * [`embed` method](/reference/api/2025-01/inference/generate-embeddings):
>   * `parameters` now accepts `Map<String, Object>` instead of `EmbedRequestParameters`.
>   * The `Embeddings` response class now has dense and sparse embeddings. You now must use `getDenseEmbedding()` or `getSparseEmbedding()`. For example, instead of `embeddings.getData().get(0).getValues()`, you would use `embeddings.getData().get(0).getDenseEmbedding().getValues()`.
> * [`rerank` method](/guides/search/rerank-results):
>   * `documents` now accepts `List<Map<String, Object>>` instead of `List<Map<String, String>>`.
>   * `parameters` now accepts `Map<String, Object>` instead of `Map<String, String>`.

### Released Go SDK v3.0.0

Released [`v3.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/go-pinecone/releases/tag/v3.0.0) of the [Pinecone Go SDK](/reference/sdks/go/overview). This version uses the latest stable API version, `2025-01`, and adds support for [sparse-only indexes](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#indexes-with-sparse-vectors).

> [!WARNING]
>
> Before upgrading to `v3.0.0`, update all relevant code to account for the following [breaking changes](/reference/api/versioning#breaking-changes). See the [`v3.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/go-pinecone/releases/tag/v3.0.0) release notes for full details.
>
> * [`embed` operation](/reference/api/2025-01/inference/generate-embeddings):
>   * `EmbedParameters` is no longer typed as a pointer.
> * [`create_index` operation](/guides/index-data/create-an-index):
>   * `CreateServerlessIndexRequest` and `CreatePodIndexRequest` structs have been updated, and fields are now classified as pointers to better denote optionality around creating specific types of indexes: `Metric`, `Dimension`, `VectorType`, and `DeletionProtection`.
> * Various data operation:
>   * `Values` in the `Vector` type are now a pointer to allow flexibility when working with sparse-only indexes.

### Released .NET SDK v3.0.0

Released [`v3.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-dotnet-client/releases/tag/3.0.0) of the [Pinecone .NET SDK](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-dotnet-client). This version uses the latest stable API version, `2025-01`, and adds support for [sparse-only indexes](/guides/index-data/indexing-overview#indexes-with-sparse-vectors).

> [!WARNING]
>
> Before upgrading to `v3.0.0`, update all relevant code to account for the following [breaking changes](/reference/api/versioning#breaking-changes). See the [`v3.0.0`](https://github.com/pinecone-io/pinecone-dotnet-client/releases/tag/3.0.0) release notes for full details.
>
> * [`embed` operation](/reference/api/2025-01/inference/generate-embeddings):
>   * The `Embedding` type has changed from a simple object to a discriminated union, supporting both `DenseEmbedding` and `SparseEmbedding`. New helper methods available on the Embedding type: `IsDense` and `IsSparse` for type checking, `AsDense()` and `AsSparse()` for type conversion, and `Match()` and `Visit()` for pattern matching.
>   * The `Parameters` property now uses `Dictionary<string, object?>?` instead of `EmbedRequestParameters`.
> * `rerank` operation:
>   * The `Document` property now uses `Dictionary<string, object?>?` instead of `Dictionary<string, string>?`.
>   * The `Parameters` property now uses `Dictionary<string, object?>?` instead of `Dictionary<string, string>?`.
